hints: Look at a single water molecule and count both what it can give and what it can receive in hydrogen bonding.
Remember that $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ has two O-H bonds to donate, plus two lone pairs on oxygen to accept.
Add the donor bonds and the acceptor bonds together to find the total maximum around one central molecule.
walkthrough:
**Draw what water has to offer**

Think of one central $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecule on its own. It has two slightly positive H atoms and one oxygen with two lone pairs.

Structure idea:
$$\text{H}-\text{O}-\text{H} \text{ with 2 lone pairs on O}$$

**Count bonds it can donate**

Each O-H hydrogen can form one hydrogen bond to the lone pair of a neighbouring water molecule. That gives 2 donated hydrogen bonds.

**Count bonds it can accept**

Each of the two lone pairs on oxygen can accept one hydrogen bond from the H atom of a different neighbouring water molecule. That gives 2 accepted hydrogen bonds.

**Add them for the maximum**

Maximum total = donated + accepted.
$$2 + 2 = 4$$
So one water molecule can be tetrahedrally surrounded by four hydrogen bonds, as seen in ice.

options.A: 1 is far too low. It ignores that water has two O-H donors and two lone pair acceptors, not just one site.
options.B: 2 counts only half the picture. Many students count only the two H atoms it donates, or only the two lone pairs it uses to accept, and forget to add both together.
options.C: 3 is a common miscount. There is no reason to lose one site, water is symmetrical with 2 donors plus 2 acceptors giving 4 in total.
options.D: 4 is correct. One $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ donates 2 hydrogen bonds through its two H atoms and accepts 2 hydrogen bonds onto its two lone pairs, for a maximum of 4.
